A ball can be struck by a piston only while it is in slot 2 or slot 3.  
• Ball 1 starts in slot 1, so it immediately rolls off: probability 0.  
• Ball 2 starts in slot 2; piston 2 fires with probability 1⁄3 before any other piston moves it to slot 1, so P=1⁄3.  
• Ball 3 starts in slot 3.  One step later:  
 – piston 3 (1⁄3) hits it immediately → success,  
 – piston 2 (1⁄3) moves it to slot 1 → failure,  
 – piston 1 (1⁄3) moves it to slot 2, where its chance of later being hit is 1⁄3.  
Therefore P(ball 3)=1⁄3+ (1⁄3)(1⁄3)=4⁄9≈0.444, larger than for balls 1 or 2.  
Any later ball eventually passes through slots 3, 2, 1 in the same pattern but spends less time in piston-eligible positions before being forced to roll off, so their probabilities decline monotonically.  Thus ball 3 gives the highest chance of being ejected by a piston.
The game starts with balls 1,2,3 in slots 1,2,3.  A ball can be struck by a piston only while it sits in slot 2 or slot 3.  
• Ball 1 is already in slot 1, so it instantly rolls off and can never be hit: P=0.
• Ball 2 begins in slot 2.  The piston that fires is equally likely to be 1,2,3; only piston 2 hits it.  Thus P=1/3.
• Ball 3 begins in slot 3.  One step later: piston 3 (1/3) hits it immediately; piston 2 (1/3) shifts it to slot 1 so it rolls off; piston 1 (1/3) moves it to slot 2, from which its hit-probability is 1/3.  Therefore P = (1/3)·1 + (1/3)·0 + (1/3)·(1/3) = 4/9 ≈ 0.444.
Every later ball must travel through the same states but with fewer opportunities (each arrives later and the sequence is strictly advancing), so their hit probabilities decrease monotonically beyond ball 3.  Consequently the maximal chance belongs to ball 3.

Sentence “At least one of us is a human” is true if there is ≥1 human, false if none. 
1. Suppose the village has ≥1 human. Then the sentence is true. Humans could say it, but vampires—who must lie—would also be uttering a true sentence, impossible. So mixture impossible.
2. Suppose all 100 are humans. Statement true, but this contradicts the observed existence of a vampire. Impossible.
3. Suppose all 100 are vampires. Statement is false; every resident lies, so each can utter this false sentence consistently. Also matches the sighting of a vampire.
Thus only logically consistent composition is 100 vampires, 0 humans.
The sentence "At least one of us is a human" is true unless there are zero humans. 1) If any humans are present, the statement is true; humans could say it, but vampires (who must lie) would also have to utter this true sentence, which they cannot. Therefore a mix of humans and vampires is impossible. 2) If all residents are human, statement true but contradicts the fact you saw a vampire. 3) If all residents are vampires, the statement is false, satisfying the lying requirement for every speaker and matching the sighting. Thus every resident must be a vampire.

The host can arrange the coins in any permutation of the thirteen triples derived from the constraints; the most damaging for any fixed set of guesses is a permutation of (6,0,24).
Because the host may permute the boxes after seeing Bob’s guesses, Bob should choose all three guesses equal: g,g,g.
For such a symmetric guess the worst-case guaranteed total is
 W(g)=2g for g≤6, W(g)=g+6 for 6<g≤24, W(g)=30 for g≥24.
Choosing any g≥24 (e.g., 24,24,24) therefore guarantees Bob wins 30 coins whatever the host does.
Each coin is worth $1 000, so the security level is 30×1 000.
Enumerating all legal coin placements shows they are permutations of the thirteen triples (6,0,24), (7,1,22), … , (18,12,0).  Because the host may permute any placement, Bob’s guess vector can be taken symmetric: (g,g,g).  For such a guess the host’s worst reply is always some permutation of (6,0,24).  Bob’s total take becomes W(g)=2g when g≤6 and W(g)=g+6 when 6<g≤24; for g≥24 the cap from the 24-coin box makes W(g)=30.  Thus the security level peaks at 30 coins, achieved by any 24≤g≤30, e.g. guesses (24,24,24).  Each coin is worth $1 000, so Bob can force 30 000 dollars.
